summary: Specifies the Endpoint Handlespace Redundancy Protocol, designed to work with ASAP to meet Reliable Server Pooling requirements. It defines procedures and message formats for a distributed, fault-tolerant registry service that stores and distributes the names of pools and their members. It is experimental.

plainLanguage.summary: ENRP lets multiple servers keep copies of the names and members of server pools. They share changes and can take over pool records when another ENRP server fails.

questions: how does enrp maintain pool information
how do enrp servers stay synchronized
what happens when an enrp server fails
subtitle: A distributed registry that keeps server-pool membership information synchronized.

tldr.problem: A single registry for server pools can fail and prevent clients from finding pool members or learning about membership changes.
tldr.mechanism: ENRP servers exchange updates and heartbeats, share handlespace data, detect silent peers, and coordinate takeover when a peer is considered failed.
tldr.outcome: The protocol defines a distributed registry for use with ASAP within a RSerPool operational scope. RFC 5353 is Experimental.

today: RFC 5353 is an Experimental RFC published in September 2008. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Distributed Handlespace
sections.content:
The Endpoint Handlespace Redundancy Protocol (ENRP) maintains the handlespace, a registry of pool handles and their member servers. It operates within a defined RSerPool scope and works with ASAP, which carries client and pool-element requests to ENRP.

ENRP servers communicate with peers to distribute pool information and update it when pool elements register, change, or leave. The protocol defines server-to-server messages; ASAP defines the interactions with pool users and pool elements.
sections.plainLanguage: ENRP is a registry shared by several servers in one operational scope. It keeps pool names and membership information available to the ASAP protocol.

sections.title: Peer Messages
sections.content:
ENRP defines messages for presence checks, requesting and returning handlespace data, updating pool members, exchanging peer lists, coordinating takeover, and reporting errors. Messages use fixed fields and typed parameters; fields are sent in network byte order.

An ENRP presence message announces that a server is available and can carry a checksum for comparing pool-element data. A handle update announces that a pool element was added, changed, or removed. A handle-table response may carry the data in several messages.
sections.plainLanguage: ENRP servers send heartbeats, exchange pool data, and announce membership changes. They also send messages to coordinate taking over records from a failed peer.

sections.title: Joining the ENRP Peer Group
sections.content:
When a server starts, it generates a nonzero 32-bit identifier and finds a mentor peer through configuration or discovery. It requests the peer list and then requests a copy of the handlespace.

The mentor may send the handlespace in multiple responses. The new server adds or updates the pool entries it receives and begins providing ENRP service after the transfer completes.
sections.plainLanguage: A new ENRP server contacts an existing peer, gets the peer list, and copies the pool information. It starts serving once it has loaded that information.

sections.title: Updates, Failure Detection and Recovery
sections.content:
When a pool element registers, changes, or leaves, its home ENRP server announces the update to peers. Each server sends periodic presence messages and records when it last heard from each peer.

If a peer remains silent beyond a configured threshold, a server probes it. If it does not respond, peers coordinate takeover so one server can become the home server for the failed peer's pool elements. Servers can compare checksums and request a new copy of a peer's entries when they detect inconsistency.
sections.plainLanguage: ENRP servers notify peers when pool membership changes and check that peers remain reachable. If a peer fails or its data differs, the servers coordinate recovery or resynchronization.

sections.title: Authentication and Data Protection
sections.content:
The RFC identifies threats including false registrations, malicious servers, replay, corrupted pool data, and eavesdropping. It requires TLS support to provide authentication, integrity, confidentiality, and replay protection for the relevant communication paths.

ENRP servers and pool elements use mutual authentication with pre-shared keys. Pool users authenticate ENRP servers using certificates. The RFC notes that multicast announcements do not have a defined security mechanism, so their source address cannot be treated as trustworthy.
sections.plainLanguage: ENRP uses TLS to authenticate servers and pool elements and to protect data from changes or observation. The RFC warns that multicast announcements are not authenticated by its specified mechanisms.
